full_judgment:
5. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was conscious of the judgment of the Appellate Division on the question of revisional jurisdiction while disposing the revisional application. In this case, the onus lies on the preemptee to prove the case of waiver as because it is the pre-emptee's assertion that the pre-emptor refused to purchase when specifically requested to do so before the sale. At first it is to be seen whether the onus of proof of such waiver has been discharged by the pre-emptee or not. The learned Single Judge referred to the evidence of the pre-emptee, namely, D. Ws. 1-3 and found that the specific deposition of D. Ws. 1-3 has not been discussed at all by the lower appellate court, wherein they categorically testified that the pre-emptor knew about, the sale from the very beginning and she having refused to purchase the case land the same was sold to the pre-emptee. Along with it, the learned Single Judge also found that the trial court as the first court of fact made proper and elaborate assessment of the deposition of both PWs and DWs, whereas the last court of fact did not advert to the evidence on record. The learned Single Judge found it to be a case of non-consideration of material evidence on record. D. W. 1 Abu Taher said in his deposition that the pre-emptor is his cousin sister and she lived in the same village and her husband knew about the transfer of the case land and requested him to purchase the case land and also told them that they would help the pre-emptor in purchasing the land. D. W. 2 A. K. M. Golzar Hossain also corroborated the statement of D. W. 1 that both the pre-emptor and her husband refused to purchase the land. This specific deposition of D. Ws. 1 and 2 was not at all considered by the last court of fact. So this non-consideration of the vital material evidence affected the merit of the case. The revisional court in the facts of the present case, correctly found that the deposition of D. Ws. 1-3 was not at all discussed and considered as has been done by the trial court. Further, the judgment of the lower appellate court is based on certain surmises and conjectures as the lower appellate court found that if the pre-emptor and her husband were requested to purchase the land before pre-emption then probably either the pre-emptor or her husband ought to have been a signatory either in the agreement or in the kabala. This is really an assumption and surmise of the lower appellate court which is not borne out by any evidence on record. There is no scope to guess this probability on the face of positive oral evidence on record. That apart, the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee are relations and live in the same village. 

 10. The appellant instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 251 of 1987 under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for pre-empting a share of the holding described in the application stating that she was a co-sharer of the holding in question by purchase 1½ decimals of land by registered kabalas dated 10.8.79 and 6.11.79 from the original owner, Md. Idris Ali and that on the death of Idris Ali his son Md. Zamir Ali, predecessor-in-interest of respondent Nos. 2-4, transferred the land under pre-emption by a registered kabala dated 18.11.1982 to the pre-emptee respondent No. 1. Md. Abu Zaher, a stranger to the holding without serving statutory notice under Section 89 of the Act upon her. 

 "I have gone through the deposition of the D. Ws. 1-3 along with the discussion made by the learned Additional District Judge in his judgment. D. W. 1 Abu Taher said in his deposition that the petitioner is his cousin sister and lived in the same village and her husband knew about the transfer of the case land and they requested him to purchase the case land and told him that they will help him in purchasing the land if required and according to their request her purchasing the case land D. W. 2 A. K. M. Gulzar Hossain Bhuiya in this deposition stated that Zamir Ali (seller) requested the petitioner (pre-emptor) at her house to purchase the case land and she and her husband refused to purchase the same at that time he (D. W. 2) and D. W. 1 was present and thereafter D. W. 1 (pre-emptee) agreed to purchase the case land. Similarly P. W. 3 said that he heard that the petitioner know about the purchase and D. W. 1 used to live in the house of the petitioner as tenant D. W. 4 Azimunnessa supported the deposition of D. Ws. 1 and 2. The learned Additional District Judge after discussing the depositions of above D. Ws observed that the D. W. 1 did not state that D. W. 2 was present at the time when requested the petitioner Zamir Ali to purchase the suit land and D. W. 4 is the sister of the transferred and D. W. 3 is not an eye witness. The specific deposition of D. Ws. 1 & 2 has not been discussed by the learned Additional District Judge and his observation has got no basis by any substantiate or cogent reason. On the contrary I find that the learned Assistant Judge discussed this matter in issue numbers 5 and 6 vividly and correctly. So it appears from the deposition of D. Ws. 2 and 3 that the petitioner (pre-emptor) knew about sale from the very beginning and she refused to purchase the case land at the first instance when she was requested for the same." 

 39. Before the trial court it appears that the petitioner deposed as P. W. 1 and she has stated her case as mentioned in the petition of the Miscellaneous Case. No objection was raised on the factum of limitation as the case was filed within time. It is the case of the defence that the property was offered to appellant by the vendor and on her refusal it was sold to opposite party No. 1 which has been denied by the pre-emptor. When the appellant denied the defence version of the case the onus lies heavily on opposite party No. 1 to prove that actually the pre-emptor was offered to purchase the land but she declined and at her instance opposite party No. 1 purchased the property. Before the trial court from the side of the petitioner no other witness was examined. It appears that the case was filed within time and the statutory deposit was also made within time, so there is no wrong in these. Only question is whether the property was offered to the pre-emptor by the vendor and on her refusal and insistence opposite party No. 1 purchased the same. 

 40. Opposite party No. 1 deposed as O. P. W. 1 before the trial court. In the entire evidence he has not stated that he purchased the property at the instance of petitioner- appellant. His specific case is that the pre-emptor was aware of his purchase. He also deposed that he was requested by P. W. 1 and her husband to purchase the property who promised to help him in the deal. It is well settled that onus to prove a fact his on the person who allege the same in such circumstances the onus lies heavily on the opposite party to prove that the pre-emptor declined to purchase the property when offered and then helped O. P. W. 1 in the deal. Before the trial court except. D. W. 1 three other witnesses have been examined but none of them deposed that they were present when the property was offered to the pre-emptor by the vendor or that P. W. 1 was instrumental in getting the property purchased by O. P. W. 1. Most important witness in this case is D. W. 4 who is the sister of the vendor, who has not stated that in her presence the vendor offered the property to P. W. 1 or that P. W. 1 asked O. P. W. 1 to purchase the property. From a consideration of the oral evidence it appears that the defence failed to discharge their onus in proving the allegation that at the instance of P. W. 1 the property was purchased by O. P. W. 1 or that the vendor offered the property to the pre-emptor on whose refusal it was sold to O. P. W. 1.
